results.term_definition: The air that surrounds us contains about 10 billion billion molecules per cubic centimeter. An ideal vacuum would be a region that contains no molecules whatsoever. In practice, we talk about a vacuum if a region contains considerably fewer particles than usual. A "high vacuum" has only one millionth of the usual number of particles per cubic centimeter, and an "ultra-high vacuum" has less than a billion particles per cubic centimeter. Most regions of outer space are even emptier than that. On average, the density of ordinary matter particles in our Universe amounts to less than one per cubic meter. What astronomers consider comparatively dense, such as a giant molecular gas cloud, is still a better vacuum than any we can produce here on Earth.
